newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Ciampi set to make only flying IMF visit.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Ciampi set to make only flying IMF visit.

text.p: Italy's Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, burdened by important business back home, will make only a flying two-day visit to Washington for the G7 and International Monetary Fund meetings.
Ciampi is due to reach Washington late on Saturday and is booked to leave for Rome on Monday evening, a day before the annual IMF conference ends.

He is expected to arrive in Italy by Tuesday, in time for the opening of debate in the lower house of parliament in the centre-left government's controversial 15.5 trillion lire ($9.1 billion) mini-budget package.
Many commentators believe Prime Minister Romano Prodi will have to call a do-or-die confidence vote to get this latest round of budget rigour through the house.

Ciampi and Prodi have insisted that the package, which includes plans to bring forward tax payments on company severance funds, will ensure that Italy is a founder member of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
But both the IMF and European Commission warned Italy this week that its latest efforts might not be enough.

The Washington-based IMF predicted that Italy's 1997 deficit would be 3.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- outside the three percent ceiling set by the Maastricht Treaty to join EMU at its planned 1999 start.
The Commission saw a 3.2 percent deficit/GDP ratio.

The forecasts angered the Italian government, which has pledged to resign if it fails to make the euro grade. "We will reply with the facts," a curt Ciampi was quoted as saying by Italian newspapers on Thursday.
But if the IMF and Commission thought 1997 was going to prove disappointing for Italy, both organisations forecast that the deficit/GDP ratio was set to widen sharply next year.
The IMF urged heavily indebted Italy to introduce structural spending cuts to the welfare state to guarantee the future stability of accounts.

Ciampi has long pressed for an overview of social spending, and with the deadline for the launch of the single European currency approaching, talks with unions on the highly sensitive subject are due to start by mid-May.

Labour Minister Tiziano Treu confirmed on Thursday that the Italian government's latest three-year economic programme (DPEF) will be ready by the end of May and will contain the broad outlines of planned social welfare reforms.
"It will show clearly where we want to go as regards pensions," Treu said on Thursday.

But hopes of enacting fresh pension reform just two years after the last overhaul, will meet tough opposition, not so much from unions but more from the hard-left Communist Refoundation, which guarantees Prodi's parliamentary majority.
One government minister suggested on Wednesday that some of the measures planned for the 1998 budget bill will be brought forward to this year to bolster accounts as soon as possible.
Treu dismissed this proposal and no one within the centre-left coalition has yet raised the spectre of a second mini-budget this year to boost Italy's EMU ambitions.
The one bright note for Italy as Ciampi heads for Washington is on the inflation front, with the IMF praising the government for its commitment to tackle price rises.
Data released this week pointed to inflation falling to 1.7 percent year-on-year in April from 2.2 percent last month.

The government is hoping that this fall will spur the Bank of Italy into cutting rates, thereby reducing the Treasury's huge debt servicing costs. Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio will also be attending the IMF meeting. $1 = 1,705 lire
